questions.title: Homework 8: Design Patterns - Introduction and Singleton
questions.question:
A junior engineer wrote this thinking it's thread-safe double-checked locking. What's actually wrong with it?
```python
import threading

class DBConnection:
    _instance = None
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        with cls._lock:
            if cls._instance is None:
                cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance
```

options.optionText: This is fully correct double-checked locking
_instance needs to be an instance variable
threading.Lock() doesn't exist in Python
This locks on every single call (not just the risky first-creation moment) because it's missing the outer, unlocked check before entering with cls._lock

questions.title: Assignment 3: Design Patterns – Introduction and Singleton
questions.question:
What will this code print?

```python
class DBConnection:
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        if cls._instance is None:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance

    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url

db1 = DBConnection("db.prod")
db2 = DBConnection("db.staging")

print(db1 is db2)
print(db1.url)
```

options.optionText: False followed by db.prod
True followed by db.prod
True followed by db.staging
False followed by db.staging

questions.title: Assignment 4: Design Patterns - Introduction and Singleton
questions.question: Why can't we just put the "only one instance" check inside __init__ instead of __new__?

options.optionText: __init__ doesn't have access to self
__init__ runs before the object is created
__init__ runs after the object already exists, so it's too late to refuse creation
__init__ cannot access class-level variables

questions.title: Assignment 5: Design Patterns – Introduction and Singleton
questions.question:
This code is meant to be a Singleton but has a bug. What's wrong?

```python
class Logger:
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance
```

options.optionText: Nothing is wrong, this is correct
It's missing an if cls._instance is None: check, so a new object is created on every single call
super().__new__(cls) should be super().__init__(cls)
_instance should be an instance variable, not a class variable
